data.content_ref: inline:The target's mechanism undermines its own claim. It asserts that choosing the highly corroborated theory 'minimizes the risk of adopting an easily falsifiable (low content) theory.' But in the Popperian framework the target invokes (empirical content, corroboration), a theory with HIGH empirical content is BY DEFINITION more easily falsifiable: it forbids more possible observations and thus has more opportunities to be refuted. So high-content theories are not less falsifiable but MORE falsifiable. The target equates 'high content' with resistance to falsification ('has proven it can withstand high-content attacks'), then in the same breath treats 'easily falsifiable' as a property of LOW-content theories to be avoided. These cannot both be true under the same notion of content. The minimax rationale is therefore incoherent: if minimizing the risk of adopting an easily falsifiable theory were the goal, one would prefer LOW content, not high content — the exact opposite of the stated preference.
